Dred Scott v. Sandford. In 1857, the Supreme Court issued what many consider its most infamous decision before the Civil War. Dred Scott was an enslaved man whose owner, John Emerson, had taken him to live in free territory. Scott sued for his freedom on grounds of his residence in those free states. Chief Justice Roger Taney ruled against him. Taney held that Scott had no right to sue because he was not a citizen. The Court stated that at the nation's founding, African Americans were viewed as having no rights which the white man was bound to respect.

The decision went further. The Court struck down the Missouri Compromise, holding that Congress had no authority to prohibit slavery in federal territories. Taney reasoned that the 14th Amendment guaranteed political equality but not social equality, allowing states wide latitude to classify citizens by race. The decision denied citizenship to all people of African descent, whether enslaved or free, undermining the legal status of free Black people in the North.

The vote was 7 to 1. The dissenter was Justice John Harlan, who argued memorably that the Constitution is color-blind and that the ruling would embolden discrimination. Taney's opinion enraged Republicans and abolitionists and deepened the sectional divide. It is widely seen as precipitating events leading directly to the Civil War.

The decision was effectively overturned by the 13th Amendment, which abolished slavery, and the 14th Amendment, which granted citizenship to all born in the United States. Yet the damage had already been done. Scott himself lived as a free man after the case but died just months after gaining his freedom.
